ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: On the left side of the circuit is a 100 V voltage source, marked with the upper end as positive and the lower end as negative; its upper end is connected through a 10 Ω resistor to the middle upper node. In the middle there is a 3 A current source, with the arrow upward, injecting from the lower common node into the middle upper node. On the right side of the middle upper node, a 20 V voltage source is connected in series, marked with the left end as positive and the right end as negative, and the right end is connected to terminal A. A resistor R was originally connected between terminal A and terminal B, and the bottom wire connects B with the lower end of the left voltage source and the lower end of the current source into a common node. Reasoning: Take B as the reference point. When A and B are short-circuited, point A and point B are at the same potential, so Va = Vb = 0 V. The 20 V voltage source is left positive and right negative, so the voltage of the middle upper node satisfies Vcentral - Va = 20 V, giving Vcentral = 20 V. The upper end of the left 100 V voltage source is 100 V relative to B, so the current flowing in the 10 Ω resistor toward the middle node is (100 - 20) / 10 = 8 A. The 3 A current source also injects 3 A into the middle node. By KCL at the middle node, these two parts of current total 8 + 3 = 11 A, and must flow through the 20 V voltage source to A, then through the A-B short-circuit line to B. Therefore the short-circuit current is 11 A.

method.method_draft: First describe the image circuit and choose B as reference. For the short-circuit condition, replace the load branch between A and B by an ideal wire, so Va = Vb = 0. From the 20 V source polarity, Vcentral − Va = 20 V, hence Vcentral = 20 V. From the left 100 V source, the node left of the 10 Ω resistor is at 100 V. The current through the 10 Ω resistor into the central node is (100 − 20)/10 = 8 A. The upward current source injects another 3 A into the central node. By KCL, the total current leaving the central node through the 20 V source toward A and then down the A-B short is 8 + 3 = 11 A, so the short-circuit current is 11 A.

planner_metadata.distinctiveness_rationale: Direct node-voltage/KCL route using the short condition at A-B; this is the natural single robust method for this circuit and is distinct enough because it relies on fixing node voltages from the ideal voltage sources before applying KCL.
planner_metadata.image_role: Read the circuit topology and values from the image: a 100 V source on the left with positive terminal at the top, a 10 Ω resistor from the 100 V top node to the central top node, a 3 A current source upward from the bottom node to the central top node, a 20 V source between the central top node and terminal A with + on the central side and − on the A side, and terminals A and B on the right where the short-circuit current is requested.
planner_metadata.text_role: Use the question text only to identify the requested quantity: the short-circuit current between terminals A and B, with answer required in amperes.
planner_metadata.knowledge_role: Use ideal-source constraints and Kirchhoff's current law. When A and B are shorted, A is at the same potential as B. The 20 V source then fixes the central node at 20 V above B. The 10 Ω resistor current is computed by Ohm's law, and KCL at the central node gives the current through the 20 V source and hence through the A-B short.
